questions.q: Is there a limit to how many tables one query can join?
options: No — you can chain as many JOIN clauses as needed
Yes, a maximum of three tables
Yes, a maximum of two JOIN clauses per query
Only two tables can ever appear in a single SELECT
questions.explain: There's no hard limit — just add another JOIN clause to bring in another table.

questions.q: Must a JOIN's ON clause always reference the very first table named in FROM?
options: No — it just needs to reference a column already available at that point in the query, which could be from an earlier JOIN
Yes, every ON clause must reference the FROM table specifically
Only the first JOIN can reference the FROM table; all others must reference each other
ON clauses cannot reference tables introduced by a previous JOIN
questions.explain: In the four-table example, the second JOIN connects to sod (from the first JOIN), not directly to soh.

questions.q: Can INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN be combined in the same query?
options: Yes — different join types can be mixed depending on what each relationship needs
No, a query must use exactly one join type throughout
Only if all tables have the same number of rows
Mixing join types always produces a Cartesian product
questions.explain: The example keeps every product via LEFT JOIN while requiring a valid subcategory via INNER JOIN — both in one query.

questions.q: Why does this course recommend qualifying every SELECT column with its table alias in a multi-table join, even when not strictly required?
options: So a reader always knows which table a column actually came from
It's required syntax once three or more tables are joined
It changes which rows are returned
It's only a performance optimization with no readability benefit
questions.explain: This is a readability/formatting discipline, extending Lesson 10's conventions to multi-table queries.

questions.q: In the four-table example query, how many JOIN clauses are needed to connect four tables?
options: Three
Four
Two
One
questions.explain: Connecting N tables generally takes N-1 JOIN clauses — one FROM table plus three JOINs makes four tables total.
